messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

CHIEF COMPLAINT: RUQ pain

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient, a 26-year-old male, presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of RUQ pain, which worsened with food. Physical exam demonstrated focal RUQ peritonitis with a positive Murphy’s sign, but no rebound or guarding. Ultrasound revealed a stone in the gallbladder neck and no pericholecystic fluid. Surgery was consulted and the patient was offered outpatient follow-up for biliary colic.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
The patient has a prior history of good health. No past medical conditions or significant illnesses were noted in the chart.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was monitored in the hospital for a brief period and discharged with a plan for outpatient follow-up for biliary colic. The following day, the patient returned to the emergency department with persistent pain and underwent cholecystectomy for cholecystitis.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to take adequate rest and avoid heavy lifting for a few days. The surgical incisions should be kept clean and dry. The patient should follow the medication regimen as prescribed. The patient is instructed to return to the hospital if there are any signs of fever, redness, swelling, or discharge at the surgical site, or if the pain persists.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will have a follow-up appointment with the surgeon in approximately one week to assess postoperative recovery and discuss any further management or treatment options.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with the appropriate medical care and follow-up plan in place.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The chief condition is acute cholecystitis caused by gallstones: a gallbladder stone seen on ultrasound, with persistent pain and inflammation requiring cholecystectomy. This is gallbladder disease, chapter K (digestive system). The stone-with-acute-cholecystitis combination is classified to the calculus of gallbladder category, K80.

CODE: K80
